articles.title: Scientists discover why damaged nerves struggle to heal
articles.summary: Scientists have identified a protein that acts like a brake on the nervous system’s ability to repair damaged connections. Blocking AHR helped injured nerve fibers regrow and improved movement and sensation in mice with nerve or spinal cord injuries. The discovery could eventually point toward new treatments designed to shift neurons from simply surviving an injury to actively rebuilding themselves.
articles.content:
Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have identified a molecular mechanism that appears to restrict the ability of injured neurons to regrow damaged axons. The findings, published in the journal Nature, suggest that blocking a protein known as the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) could promote nerve regeneration and improve recovery after damage to peripheral nerves or the spinal cord.

Axons are long extensions of nerve cells, or neurons, that transmit signals throughout both the central and peripheral nervous systems. These fibers are essential for communication between nerve cells. When axons are damaged or severed, recovery depends heavily on whether neurons can rebuild those connections.

Why Damaged Nerves Struggle To Regrow

In adult mammals, however, neurons have only a limited capacity to regenerate their axons. As a result, injuries involving nerves or the spinal cord can cause long-lasting or permanent problems with movement and sensation. Understanding what prevents stronger regrowth has been a major challenge for researchers.

The new research points to AHR as an important regulator of how neurons respond to injury.

"When neurons are injured, they must deal with stress while also trying to regrow their axons," said Hongyan Zou, MD, PhD, Professor of Neurosurgery, and Neuroscience, at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and the study's senior author. "We discovered that AHR functions like a brake that shifts neurons toward managing stress rather than rebuilding damaged connections."

Researchers found that active AHR signaling suppresses axon growth. When they removed AHR from neurons or used drugs to block its activity, damaged axonal fibers regenerated more successfully. In mouse models involving peripheral nerve damage and spinal cord injury, suppressing AHR also led to better recovery of movement and sensation.

A Tradeoff Between Survival and Repair

Additional experiments helped explain why AHR has this effect. Following an injury, the protein supports a protective response that helps neurons maintain protein quality control -- a process known as proteostasis. This system helps injured neurons withstand cellular stress, but it also limits the production of new proteins required for rebuilding axons.

Without active AHR, neurons appear to change priorities. They increase the production of new proteins and turn on biological pathways associated with growth and axon regeneration. The researchers found that this response also relies on another factor called HIF-1α, which helps control genes involved in metabolism and tissue repair.

"This discovery shows that neurons use AHR to balance survival and regeneration," Dr. Zou explained. "By releasing this brake, we can push neurons into a state that favors repair."

An Unexpected Role for a Toxin Sensor

AHR was first identified because of its ability to detect environmental toxins and pollutants, termed xenobiotics. The latest findings indicate that its role extends beyond environmental sensing. Inside neurons, AHR appears to connect responses to the surrounding environment with the cellular processes that determine whether damaged axons can regenerate.

The discovery could eventually have therapeutic implications. Several drugs designed to inhibit AHR are already undergoing clinical trials for other conditions. That raises the possibility that researchers could one day investigate similar drugs as treatments for injuries involving peripheral nerves or the spinal cord.

Moving Toward Potential Treatments

The work remains at an early stage, and additional research will be necessary before AHR targeting could be considered for patients. Future studies will test how well AHR inhibitors work across different forms of neural injury, identify appropriate treatment timing and dosage, and examine how suppressing the protein affects other cells involved in the injury response.

The Mount Sinai team also plans to investigate AHR-blocking drugs and gene-therapy approaches that reduce AHR activity specifically in neurons. Researchers hope to determine whether these strategies can further enhance axon regeneration and improve recovery following spinal cord injury, stroke, or other neurological diseases.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery identifying a protein that limits nerve regeneration and shows that blocking this protein can promote nerve repair and functional recovery in animal models. This breakthrough has broad implications for developing new treatments for nerve and spinal cord injuries, which affect many people worldwide. The article provides detailed context on the mechanism, experimental evidence, and potential therapeutic applications, fulfilling criteria for inspiring good news with meaningful health impact.

articles.title: Your sleep may be hiding an early clue to Alzheimer’s
articles.summary: Frequent micro-awakenings during sleep were linked to higher genetic risk for Alzheimer’s in healthy middle-aged adults who had no symptoms. The discovery raises the possibility that subtle changes during sleep could offer an early warning signal years before memory problems appear.
articles.content:
Could subtle changes during sleep reveal vulnerability to Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems become noticeable? Researchers at ULiège, supported by the Stop Alzheimer's Foundation, are investigating whether the sleeping brain may contain early clues.

Scientists from the University of Liège (GIGA Neurosciences) examined sleep patterns in more than 500 healthy people. Among participants in middle age, more frequent nighttime micro awakenings were associated with a higher genetic risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. That relationship was not detected among younger adults.

The findings, published in the journal Sleep, raise the possibility that sleep measurements could eventually help researchers identify people who may be more vulnerable to Alzheimer's before symptoms develop.

Looking for Alzheimer's Clues Before Symptoms

Researchers have spent years investigating connections between disturbed sleep and neurodegenerative diseases. The University of Liège study adds another piece to that research by suggesting that the relationship between sleep and Alzheimer's risk may begin well before recognizable symptoms emerge.

Because genetics play a partial role in Alzheimer's disease (Alzheimer's disease is neither purely hereditary nor entirely independent of genes), the researchers calculated a polygenic risk (i.e., summarizing the combined influence of your genes on your probability of developing a given disease in a single figure) for more than 500 healthy participants.

Most were young adults (aged 18 to 31), while the study also included an older group (aged 50 to 69). Importantly, the polygenic risk measured in the study remained low and cannot determine whether any particular person will eventually develop Alzheimer's disease.

The researchers then compared these genetic risk estimates with different characteristics of each participant's sleep.

Tiny Awakenings During the Night

The analysis revealed an association between genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease and the frequency of nighttime micro awakenings. These are very brief bursts of brain activity that can interrupt the normal sleep cycle without causing someone to become fully awake.

Among the younger participants, researchers found no connection between these micro awakenings and Alzheimer's genetic risk. A different pattern appeared in the older group. Participants who experienced more frequent micro awakenings also tended to have higher genetic risk, despite being healthy, relatively young and free of Alzheimer's symptoms.

"These micro-awakenings are therefore not insignificant," emphasizes Puneet Talwar, a researcher at the GIGA ULiège laboratory, "certain profiles could promote the accumulation of proteins involved in Alzheimer's disease and be associated with increased vulnerability."

A Tiny Brain Region Draws Attention

The researchers also examined the locus coeruleus, a tiny area deep within the brainstem that is roughly the size of a grain of rice. It plays an important role in regulating wakefulness, attention, and sleep.

"This region is difficult to observe, but it appears to play a role in the early mechanisms linked to the disease," explains Gilles Vandewalle, co-director of the GIGA CRC In Vivo Imaging technology platform and Fund for Scientific Research - FNRS Research Director at ULiège.

In 2025, a preliminary study carried out with the 7-Tesla MRI scanner at the ULiège platform allowed the team to examine the locus coeruleus in greater detail. The researchers found that characteristics of sleep quality (speed of falling asleep, depth) were associated with the condition of the brainstem beginning at a young age.

They also found that healthy functioning of the locus coeruleus was related to the quality of REM sleep, a stage of sleep that plays an important role in memory.

The locus coeruleus is especially interesting to Alzheimer's researchers because it is among the earliest brain regions where abnormal protein deposits can appear. Such deposits may begin accumulating as early as adolescence, although scientists still do not fully understand what these early changes mean.

Could Sleep Become an Early Alzheimer's Marker?

Taken together, the findings point toward possible new approaches for Alzheimer's screening and prevention. In the future, analyzing sleep could potentially complement other methods for identifying people who may be vulnerable to the disease before symptoms become apparent.

"Sleep could become an accessible marker for the early identification of vulnerable individuals," adds Gilles Vandewalle.

Researchers are also interested in whether improving sleep could eventually help prevent or slow disease progression among people with a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's.

"This research shows that sleep is not only an indicator of health, but also a potential lever for intervention," adds Lucie Leroux, head of French-speaking activities at the Stop Alzheimer's Foundation.

More than 220,000 people in Belgium are affected by Alzheimer's disease. For now, however, the new findings show statistical associations rather than proof that particular sleep patterns cause or predict the disease. Additional research will be needed to confirm the results, and the findings cannot currently be used to determine whether an individual will develop Alzheimer's.

Even so, the research provides another glimpse into changes that may occur long before Alzheimer's becomes clinically visible and underscores the value of basic research aimed at understanding and, eventually, anticipating the disease.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery linking sleep patterns to early genetic risk indicators for Alzheimer's disease, which could lead to earlier detection and potential intervention. The study involves a large sample size and offers meaningful implications for public health by potentially enabling earlier identification and prevention strategies for a widespread neurodegenerative disease.

articles.title: Exclusive video of world’s first echidna puggle to be born at a university
articles.summary: Echidnas are a difficult animal to breed in captivity, but scientists in Sydney have now managed it, which could improve our understanding of the evolution of pregnancy in mammals
articles.content:
Echidnas are a difficult animal to breed in captivity, but scientists in Sydney have now managed it, which could improve our understanding of the evolution of pregnancy in mammals

A baby echidna – one of Australia’s egg-laying monotremes – has been born and reared in a university for the first time. The baby, known as a puggle, was born earlier this month and has now been removed from its mother’s pouch for its first weigh-in. The scientists hope that, by researching this puggle and other echidnas, we will finally be able to understand some fundamental questions about the evolution of pregnancy in mammals.

The short-beaked echidna (Tachyglossus aculeatus), also known as the spiny anteater, has proved to be an extremely difficult species to breed in captivity. In spite of numerous attempts, a dedicated research colony had never been successfully established, though several zoos and wildlife sanctuaries have bred the species.

Now, Oliver Griffith at Macquarie University in Sydney and his team are successfully rearing a puggle, which is thought to be the first in the world born at a university. This week, it had become big enough that they felt confident in temporarily removing it from its mother’s pouch for weighing, which New Scientist was invited to witness.

Advertisement

T. aculeatus is one of only five known species of monotremes, a group of mammals that lay eggs. The others are three different species of echidna in New Guinea and the platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus). Most researchers believe monotremes are an ancient mammalian lineage that predate placentals.

Studying the chemical composition of echidna eggs may reveal how different they are to those of reptiles, which could give clues on when mammals and reptiles diverged, says Griffith. “We’ll look at eggshell proteins in the echidna and compare that to eggshell proteins in reptiles and try to work out: do they have the same origin or did they evolve independently?”

Kootear, a female echidna, was anaesthetised at Macquarie University in Sydney earlier this week so her offspring could be removed from her pouch for weighing James Woodford

Five females and four males are in captivity at Macquarie University. In early August, Griffith and his colleagues noticed that the puggle’s mother, named Kootear, had stopped eating and moving for around 10 days, a sign that birth is imminent. Pregnant echidnas move their egg into a pouch, where it incubates while the female is fasting and immobilised.

“We had an inkling that she may have laid an egg,” says Griffith. “So, three weeks ago, we looked into her pouch and we found what was a very tiny, almost jelly-bean-sized baby that had hatched only a couple of days before.”

A week later, the team checked the pouch again and found the puggle had surged in size. “It had grown a crazy amount actually, and it was surprising to see it so much bigger in just seven days,” says Griffith.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter

When it was checked for the third time, the researchers anaesthetised Kootear so the puggle could be briefly removed. They found it weighed 36 grams and was starting to look like an echidna, albeit one without any spines or fur.

“Before this point, you couldn’t obviously see it was an echidna – you might confuse it with a platypus puggle or, maybe even, just because it’s a pink thing, you might think it was a kangaroo baby,” says Griffith. “But today you could really see the shape of an echidna – the beak, the feet, everything.”

Echidnas can live for more than 50 years in captivity. The university’s echidnas are unlikely to ever be released into the wild. “This is a long-term research programme,” says Griffith. “I’ve set this up to be sort of a career’s worth of research, and this puggle may well outlive me.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports the successful captive breeding of echidnas at a university, a significant scientific achievement that can advance understanding of mammalian pregnancy evolution. This breakthrough has broad scientific and educational significance, with potential long-term benefits for evolutionary biology and conservation research.

articles.title: How one of the 'most powerful hacks' to control stress actually works
articles.summary: We spoke to experts about how the breathing technique used by soldiers and influencers works.
articles.content:
Powerless to help after catastrophic earthquakes struck her hometown of La Guaira in Venezuela two months ago, Maria Medina struggled to sleep.

She was more than 1,500 miles away in Florida, USA - where she has lived for the last 15 years - and was racked with worry for family and friends.

Box breathing helped her combat sleepless nights.

"In moments where I feel that there isn't much that I can do, like lying in bed at night and staring at the ceiling... I know it's going to help me," she says.

The 31-year-old first came across box breathing in 2020. She was studying for a master's degree while working full-time and the stress of doing both became too much once the Covid pandemic hit.

She sought help from a therapist who showed her how to box breathe.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the positive impact of a breathing technique, box breathing, which helps individuals manage stress and anxiety, demonstrating a practical and accessible method with broad relevance for mental health improvement.
articles.personality_title: How box breathing helps people manage stress in tough times
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people feel stressed and anxious during difficult events, like natural disasters or busy life moments. Finding simple ways to calm down can improve sleep and focus.

**What happened** – Maria Medina, who lives in Florida but worried about her family after earthquakes hit her hometown in Venezuela, used a breathing method called box breathing to help her sleep. She first learned this technique in 2020 when she was stressed from studying and working during the pandemic.

**Impact** – Box breathing is a simple way to reduce stress by controlling your breath. It can help calm the mind and body, making it easier to sleep or stay focused. People like Maria find it useful when they feel overwhelmed and powerless.

**What's next step** – More people might try box breathing as a quick and easy tool to manage stress. Experts could teach it in schools, workplaces, or therapy to help others handle anxious moments.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Box breathing offers a simple, effective way to calm stress and improve sleep during challenging times.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment la respiration en boîte aide à gérer le stress en période difficile
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup de personnes ressentent du stress et de l'anxiété lors d'événements difficiles, comme des catastrophes naturelles ou des périodes chargées. Trouver des moyens simples de se calmer peut améliorer le sommeil et la concentration.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Maria Medina, qui vit en Floride mais s'inquiétait pour sa famille après des tremblements de terre dans sa ville natale au Venezuela, a utilisé une méthode de respiration appelée respiration en boîte pour mieux dormir. Elle a découvert cette technique en 2020, quand le stress lié aux études et au travail pendant la pandémie est devenu trop important.

**Impact** – La respiration en boîte est une méthode simple pour réduire le stress en contrôlant sa respiration. Elle aide à calmer l'esprit et le corps, facilitant le sommeil et la concentration. Des personnes comme Maria la trouvent utile quand elles se sentent dépassées.

**Étape suivante** – De plus en plus de personnes pourraient essayer la respiration en boîte comme outil rapide et facile pour gérer le stress. Les experts pourraient l'enseigner dans les écoles, au travail ou en thérapie pour aider d'autres personnes.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – La respiration en boîte est un moyen simple et efficace pour calmer le stress et améliorer le sommeil en période difficile.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo la respiración en caja ayuda a manejar el estrés en momentos difíciles
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas sienten estrés y ansiedad durante eventos difíciles, como desastres naturales o momentos muy ocupados. Encontrar formas simples de calmarse puede mejorar el sueño y la concentración.

**Qué pasó** – María Medina, que vive en Florida pero estaba preocupada por su familia tras terremotos en su ciudad natal en Venezuela, usó una técnica de respiración llamada respiración en caja para ayudarla a dormir. Aprendió esta técnica en 2020 cuando el estrés de estudiar y trabajar durante la pandemia fue mucho.

**Impacto** – La respiración en caja es una forma sencilla de reducir el estrés controlando la respiración. Ayuda a calmar la mente y el cuerpo, facilitando el sueño y la concentración. Personas como María la encuentran útil cuando se sienten abrumadas.

**Próximo paso** – Más personas podrían probar la respiración en caja como una herramienta rápida y fácil para manejar el estrés. Los expertos podrían enseñarla en escuelas, trabajos o terapias para ayudar a otros.

**Frase clave** – La respiración en caja es una forma simple y efectiva para calmar el estrés y mejorar el sueño en tiempos difíciles.
